planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall into consistently moist, humus-rich soil, setting crowns just at soil level and spacing them a foot apart.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil and mulch well to keep roots cool, since this low, mounding astilbe will scorch quickly if it dries out. Provide morning sun with afternoon shade in most climates, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep blooming strong. Its finely cut, glossy foliage stays low and ferny while wiry stems carry shell-pink plumes above the mound in mid to late summer. The compact habit makes it an excellent edging plant along shaded paths or at the front of a woodland border where taller astilbes would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Set divisions or potted plants in spring after the soil has warmed, in rich, moisture-retentive soil, and water deeply until established.

directions: Grow in fertile, consistently damp soil enriched with compost, and keep a layer of mulch over the roots to buffer summer heat and moisture swings. Filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade brings out the best flower color without scorching the fine foliage. This older Arends hybrid produces soft salmon-pink plumes over mounds of dark green, deeply cut leaves in early summer, blooming a bit ahead of many other astilbe cultivars. Its gentle color and reliable performance make it a good companion for hostas and ferns along a shaded stream bank or border edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, organically rich soil, spacing plants about a foot apart and watering in well.

directions: Site in humus-rich soil that stays reliably moist and add a couple inches of mulch to prevent the shallow root system from drying between waterings. Part shade with protection from hot afternoon sun keeps the bright pink plumes from fading quickly. One of the earliest-blooming Arendsii astilbes, it sends up dense, bubblegum-pink flower spikes over glossy dark green foliage in early summer, extending the astilbe bloom season when paired with later cultivars. It reads well massed along a shaded path or combined with hostas and heucheras for season-long texture.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plants in spring or early fall in well-drained soil, keeping the crown at soil level to prevent rot.

directions: Plant in loose, well-drained soil amended with compost, since heucheras dislike heavy, waterlogged ground, and mulch lightly to keep the crown from heaving in winter. Morning sun with afternoon shade gives the richest silver overlay while protecting leaves from summer scorch. This Terra Nova selection carries silvery-gray leaves etched with dark green veins and maroon undersides, forming a tidy mound that holds its color from spring through fall. Its calm, patterned foliage pairs well with brighter gold or burgundy coral bells and works nicely as edging along a shaded walkway.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Lime Marmalade Heuchera (Chartreuse Ruffled Coral Bells)

planting.note: Set divisions or potted plants in spring in rich, well-drained soil, spacing about a foot apart and watering consistently while roots establish.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil and avoid heavy clay or standing water, which quickly rots the shallow crown of most coral bells. Bright, indirect light or a few hours of morning sun keeps the ruffled leaves glowing chartreuse without bleaching them out in hot afternoon exposure. Its large, deeply lobed, lime-green leaves stay vivid through the growing season and take on warmer amber tones in cool fall weather, with airy sprays of tiny cream flowers in early summer. The vivid color makes it a strong focal point in a shaded container or border where it lights up darker corners of the garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in loose, well-drained soil, setting the crown level with the surrounding soil to avoid rot.

directions: Site in humus-rich soil with good drainage and water regularly the first season while the fibrous root system spreads, then taper off once established. Part shade suits this cultivar best, since deep near-black coloring can fade in intense sun but the plant still needs enough light to stay compact and full. Ruffled, glossy leaves emerge nearly black with a subtle red undertone, holding color through the season better than many dark heucheras, and thin stems lift small white flowers above the foliage in early summer. Its dramatic, dark foliage makes a striking contrast plant next to silver brunnera or golden sedges in a shaded bed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Redstone Falls Heucherella (Trailing Copper-Red Foamy Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow the trailing stolons room to spread.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich soil and keep it consistently watered, since this trailing selection has shallower roots than mounding heucherellas and dries out faster. Filtered shade or morning sun brings out the deepest copper-red foliage tones while protecting leaves from midday heat. Unlike most upright heucherella cultivars, this one spreads by trailing stolons that root as they go, forming a dense mat of maple-like leaves that shift from copper-red to green through the seasons. It works especially well cascading over a shaded rock wall, spilling from a container, or knitting together as a groundcover beneath taller shade perennials.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and water well until new growth appears.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and provide shelter from hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the delicate cream leaf margins. Deep shade to part shade suits this cultivar well, and a summer mulch layer helps keep roots cool and moist. Heart-shaped green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy white, giving a softer, lacier look than solid-silver brunnera cultivars, and sprays of tiny sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage in spring. It brightens deep shade beds nicely when paired with dark-leaved heucheras or ferns for contrast.

common_name: Little Rocket Ligularia (Compact Spiked Leopard Plant)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently wet to moist soil, spacing clumps a couple feet apart to allow for their spreading habit.

directions: Plant in heavy, fertile soil that stays consistently wet, such as along a pond edge or low spot, since ligularias wilt dramatically in dry conditions even in shade. Morning sun with shade from the hot afternoon reduces wilting and leaf scorch during summer heat. A more compact form of the well-known 'The Rocket' ligularia, this cultivar produces the same near-black stems and bold, triangular toothed leaves but stays shorter and better behaved in smaller gardens, with narrow spikes of yellow flowers rising above the foliage in mid to late summer. It brings dramatic vertical form and bold texture to a shaded bog garden or streamside planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into loose, humus-rich woodland soil, spacing them close together to encourage the rhizomes to knit into a groundcover more quickly.

directions: Plant into rich, well-drained woodland soil with a good layer of leaf litter or compost worked in, and water regularly the first season while the spreading rhizomes establish. Full to dappled shade under deciduous trees matches its native habitat, and once settled it tolerates the dry shade common under mature trees better than many sedges. Slender, arching blue-green leaves emerge early in spring and spread gradually by rhizomes to form a loose, natural-looking carpet, with inconspicuous flowers in April. It makes an easy, low-maintenance native alternative to turf or pachysandra beneath trees and along woodland paths.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil under tree cover, spacing plants closely for faster groundcover coverage.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, mimicking the rich floodplain and upland woods where it grows naturally, and mulch with leaf litter to retain moisture. Deep to dappled shade suits it best, and once established it handles brief dry spells better than many woodland sedges. This diminutive, tufted sedge forms neat, grass-like clumps of soft green foliage that stay low and tidy without spreading aggressively, making it easy to tuck between other woodland perennials. Its fine texture and small scale make it a good choice for shaded rock gardens or as a filler between hostas, trilliums, and other shade natives.
